claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: Fix a plane embedding and restrict it to the K_{2,|B|} formed by p,q and B. For k=|B|≥3 this skeleton is bipartite and 2-connected, with k+2 vertices and 2k edges. Euler's formula gives k faces. Every facial boundary has length at least four, while their total length is 4k, so every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. The embedded image of any component outside the skeleton, together with the interiors of its attachment edges, is connected and disjoint from the skeleton, hence lies in one skeleton face. Its B-neighbors are therefore among that face's two consecutive gates. For k≤2 the bound is immediate.
claims.search_method: Direct plane-embedding proof, including separate checks of |B|=0,1,2 and the facial-boundary argument for |B|≥3.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: Conditions (i) and (ii) give an immediate exit or arrival at a gate whose two exit edges cannot both be deleted in one response. Under (iii), after moving to w the two triples {wb_i,b_ip,b_iq} are edge-disjoint, so one deletion leaves one triple intact; after entering that gate, at least one exit edge survives the next deletion. Conversely, if none holds, the first destination w is outside the skeleton and sees at most one boundary gate of its outside component. By claim 0 that component has at most two gates. Nemesis prepares the visible gate, or an arbitrary boundary gate if none is visible. On every later move inside that component, at most one unprepared boundary gate can newly become immediately accessible, so Nemesis prepares it. Upon entry into a prepared gate, Nemesis deletes its other exit edge. Independence of B then forces the fugitive to leave through an outside component having the dead gate and at most one further gate, which can again be prepared immediately. Deleting the just-traversed edge supplies a legal harmless choice whenever no preparation is needed. Thus no unprepared gate is entered and eventual escape is impossible. Marking B and scanning adjacency lists implements the three tests in linear time. Exact enumeration also found agreement on 19,252 starting positions across 2,514 small graphs satisfying the two-gate component property.
claims.search_method: Adversarial invariant proof plus exact integer-bitmask minimax enumeration of small two-gate instances.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: Replace each regular-exit edge vx by an edge from v to its own fresh exit leaf and retain every regular-regular edge. Before escape, legal fugitive moves and Nemesis deletions correspond edge-for-edge; moving across a replaced incidence ends the game in both instances, and a regular position has an exit path before a deletion exactly when its transformed position has a fresh-leaf path. Hence outcomes are preserved. If the regular induced graph is a forest, attaching distinct leaves keeps every relevant component a tree. If every regular vertex originally has degree at most three, its degree is unchanged and every new exit has degree one, so the transformed graph has maximum degree three. The authorized source's linear-time theorem for trees and simple maximum-degree-three graphs then applies, and the transformation is linear-sized. Exhaustive comparison of original and exit-split games passed for 3,208 regular starts across all 1,096 simple graphs with two exits and at most three regular vertices, including exit-exit edges and disconnected cases.
claims.search_method: Direct game-history-preservation proof, structural reduction to the source theorem, and exhaustive exact minimax comparison of small instances.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: The graph is simple and has exactly the stated seven vertices and two exits. Exact minimax confirms that s→c wins. If the first deletion is bc, c→z leaves the two edge-disjoint escape triples through a and b, so the second deletion can spoil at most one. Otherwise c→b is available; a surviving bp or bq wins immediately, while deletion of both requires the first two deletions to be exactly bp,bq, leaving ba,ap,aq intact and permitting escape through a. A combinatorial rotation system has five faces, and 7−10+5=2, certifying planarity. After splitting exit incidences, only s and c are within distance one of s. Vertex s has only one incident edge. A tree rooted at c cannot use regular leaf s, so its children must be b,z; then z, being regular with parent c, would require children a,b, repeating b across the root branches. Exhaustive enumeration of every edge subset confirms zero binary escape trees rooted at s or c.
claims.witness: Vertices p,q,s,a,b,c,z with edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs; the persisted checker prints a genus-zero rotation certificate and verifies all ten first-deletion branches.
claims.search_method: Exact Boolean minimax, exhaustive deletion branching, exhaustive binary-subtree enumeration, and combinatorial rotation-system enumeration without floating point.

claims.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
claims.evidence: With the existential quantifier scoped over a chosen surviving move vw, the disjunction exactly matches the rules: reaching an exit wins before Nemesis acts; otherwise every legal deletion must avoid immediate disconnection and leave a recursively winning state. Induction on |E−D| proves the recurrence because every nonterminal recursive call adds exactly one edge to D. There are at most n·2^m states and only polynomial work per transition, yielding O*(2^m) time. For a planar simple graph with n≥3, m≤3n−6, hence O*(2^m)⊆O*(8^n); the smaller exactly-two-exit cases are trivial. Depth-first evaluation has at most m recursive levels and polynomial-size masks and frames, establishing PSPACE membership. A separately coded alternating-turn semantics agreed with the recurrence on all 5,404 starts in all 1,098 simple graphs of order two through five.
claims.search_method: Well-founded induction and state-count analysis, supplemented by exhaustive exact comparison with an independently phased move/delete game tree.

target_evidence: The exact target requires either a polynomial-time algorithm or a matching hardness result for all planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. The draft proves neither: its recurrence is exponential, and its linear algorithms cover only restricted subclasses. The verified cyclic decomposition, exact same-neighborhood classification, two additional linear-time subclasses, and planar counterexample are nevertheless material and directly target-relevant progress. The final writeup expressly calls the result partial and identifies the unresolved general core, so it does not overclaim target coverage. Accordingly the target verdict is VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS and claimed_resolution=PARTIAL is ACCURATE.
